query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding 1–3 atomic % Cu during synthesis of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy, with subsequent thermal treatment to precipitate Cu‐rich nanoparticles along grain boundaries, will improve its mechanical integrity (by enhancing crack deflection and bridging) without reducing its large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits a strong caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field conditions but suffers from poor integrity and a tendency to crack.
generation.intervention: Introduce 1–3 atomic % Cu into the alloy during synthesis and apply controlled thermal processing to encourage the formation and uniform dispersion of Cu-rich nanoparticles along the grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: The alloy will be operated under the same applied magnetic and pressure fields and temperature regimes typical for its caloric evaluation. Mechanical loading (e.g., compression tests) should simulate the conditions used in prior studies on similar materials.
generation.structural_mediator: Cu‐rich nanoparticles that segregate to the grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Cu-rich nanoparticles at the grain boundaries are expected to act as barriers to crack initiation and propagation by deflecting cracks or bridging microcracks. This structural refinement should improve the resistance to brittle failure while maintaining the intrinsic caloric behavior associated with the alloy's phase transitions.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in compressive strength and fracture toughness (potentially approaching improvements similar to those seen with epoxy or low-melting In composites) without a measurable reduction in the thermally driven caloric response.
generation.baseline: The unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy shows high caloric performance but exhibits poor structural integrity and a propensity for cracking under loading.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of this intervention is expected under the operational conditions typical for caloric measurements (applied-field, pressure-field regimes, and conventional temperature exposure) and within the safe compositional limits that preserve the alloy’s high-entropy and caloric characteristics. The annealing temperature and time must be optimized to produce the Cu nanoparticle dispersion without triggering detrimental phase changes.
generation.uncertainty: The precise nanoparticle size, distribution, and volume fraction required to balance improved mechanical integrity with unaltered caloric performance are not yet defined. Additionally, the potential for Cu to interact with the caloric mechanism in unforeseen ways remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy: one set with a 1–3 atomic % Cu addition (with designed thermal processing to form Cu‐rich nanoparticles) and one control set without Cu. Subject both sets to identical applied-field and pressure-field cycling, measure their caloric responses, and perform standardized compressive strength and fracture toughness tests. Additionally, conduct microstructural analysis (using SEM/TEM) to confirm the presence and distribution of Cu-rich nanoparticles.
measurements: Caloric response metrics (e.g., temperature change, entropy change)
Microstructural characterization (e.g., nanoparticle size/distribution, grain boundary integrity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cu-doped samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (compressive strength and fracture toughness) relative to the control, or if the caloric response of the modified alloy is degraded compared to the unmodified sample under identical test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The crack exhibits a nanosized zigzag propagation path, in which many nanoscale crack-deflection and grain-bridging phenomena are clearly observed. It is worth mentioning that these nanoscale crack-deflection and grain-bridging phenomena can dissipate a large magnitude of energy, improving the fracture toughness.
